case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court upheld the then-current MCL 712A.19b(5), holding the trial court may find termination clearly not in the child's best interests on the whole record without assigning the parent any burden of producing best-interest evidence, and reviewed both the statutory ground and best interests for clear error.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms the trial court may decline to terminate and leave the case open on the whole record even after a statutory ground is proved.
key_cases.quote: Subsection 19b(5) allows the court to find that termination is "clearly not in the child's best interests" despite the establishment of one or more grounds for termination.

key_cases.holding: The Court held the trial court clearly erred in terminating the rights of a mother who had fulfilled every requirement of her parent-agency agreement, because compliance is affirmative evidence of her ability to provide proper care and custody.
key_cases.relevance: Where the parent has satisfied the plan and the alleged condition is resolved, the case should close rather than proceed to termination.
key_cases.quote: the parent's compliance with the parent-agency agreement is evidence of her ability to provide proper care and custody

key_cases.holding: The Court reinstated the probate court's termination order, holding that findings in a termination case may be set aside only if clearly erroneous and that MCR 2.613(C) requires deference to the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility.
key_cases.relevance: The same deference governs review of a decision not to terminate, which is why dismissals and non-terminations are rarely disturbed on appeal.
key_cases.quote: An appellate court should not reverse the findings of a trial court in such a case unless its findings are clearly erroneous.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and held that MCL 712A.19b(3)(l), which permits termination on the bare fact of a prior involuntary termination, creates an irrebuttable presumption of parental unfitness and therefore fails to comport with due process, and it declined to adopt a saving construction.
key_cases.relevance: Where the only ground pleaded is the earlier termination and the agency cannot prove unremedied abuse or neglect under subsection (3)(i), the petition cannot support termination and the case must return to the trial court.
key_cases.quote: As written, MCL 712A.19b(3)(l) provides no way to rebut this presumption of unfitness, assuming the fact of the prior involuntary termination.
